You save that for old things and roads don't feel old to you. They feel like they belong to cars, trucks, freight. So who built the first roads and why? You'll probably reach for one of three. The Romans, or traders moving goods, or no one, until someone had a wheel. All three feel right. All three, as far as we can tell, are wrong. The earliest road builders we can name weren't fighting distance. They were fighting water. The same answer turns up in Northern Germany. Some of the oldest paths sit near a lake called the Dummer. One of them, a path labeled PR 31, crossed a bog called the Campomor. Egypt built for something else entirely. The quarry is called Wieden El Farris, and the paving is whatever lay close. Basalt, a hard dark lava stone, limestone, sandstone, and slabs of petrified wood, dead trees turn to stone late as pavement. And in that German bog country, the oldest road beats the oldest wheel by some 2,000 years. The wheel is not the parent of the road. The wheel is a guest on it.
